To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the isolated CH(3) I molecule undergoes two stages of intramo- lecular vibrational relaxation, a fast component in 2-5 ps and a slow component in about 400 picoseconds.

vibrational relaxation of the isolated molecule is dominated by a fast component of intramolecular energy flow that occurs in a time scale of a few picoseconds, while in liquid solutions, the vibrational energy is transferred to the solvent in a time scale on the order of 10 ps.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of vibrational relaxation in isolated molecules, in liquids, and at liquid surfaces.
the dynamics of intramolecular energy redistribution and energy flow between molecules in condensed media.
the relaxation dynamics of molecules following excitation to the C-H stretch vibrational overtones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
vibrational relaxation of the C-H stretching overtone in CH(3) I in the gas phase is dominated by IVR and that in solution is dominated by IET.
the vibrational dynamics of the CH(3) group in the gas phase is not significantly altered by the solvent.
the vibrational relaxation of CH(3)(I) in solution is dominated by IET and that IVR is not a major relaxation mechanism in this system.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the relaxation dynamics of CH3I following excitation in the C-H stretch region is governed by the interplay between the vibrational state structure and the solvent environment, and that the solvent plays a role that is more than just a heat bath.
vibrational relaxation in CH(3)X molecules (X = I, Br, and Cl) occurs in three steps.

the C-H stretch vibration of CH(3)-I is coupled to the C-I stretch and C-I-I bend modes, and that the C-I-I bend mode is coupled to the CH(3) umbrella mode in the gas phase, and to the C-I-I stretch mode in the liquid phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the vibrational relaxation in CH(3)X (where X = Cl, Br, I) molecules is very different from that in the CH(4) molecule and in other small hydrocarbons.

the vibrational dynamics of molecules in solution can be understood by considering the interplay of the vibrational relaxation pathways that are available in the isolated molecule and the solvent environment, and not simply by considering the isolated molecule and solvent separately.
the vibrational state structure of CH(3I) is robust to changes in its environment.
